itemized_evaluation.justification: The paper provides explicit conflict of interest and funding disclosures in Section 6: 'Funding: zero received; independent research. In accordance with Darrell Huff's Question 1 standards and ICMJE guidelines, the author provides full and complete funding disclosures: this study received no commercial sponsorships, no venture funding, and no industry grants.' and under Competing interests: 'D.S. is the founder and a beneficiary of FreshCredit Inc... FreshCredit Inc holds granted US utility patents...'

The document is titled 'Whitepaper' and self-identifies as part of a preprint/self-archived collection ('This document contains all of the stack’s financial content; the companion protocol preprint contains none'; 'OSF / Zenodo Archive (Release v4.3, Accession: https://github.com/devonshigaki/trust-stack-research-collection/releases/tag/v4.3)'). It is not published in a peer-reviewed journal or an institutional repository with clear peer-review credentials.

Prior works and cited statistics are represented with extreme rigor, actively correcting stale frames and labeling vendor bias. In §1.1: 'The Bureau’s 2015 estimate... was revised by its own June 2025 technical correction... Where the two frames disagree on market size, this document uses the corrected CFPB figures everywhere.' In §1.3: 'A widely circulated claim that 95% of synthetic identities pass onboarding undetected, attributed to Thomson Reuters across vendor blogs, could not be traced to any primary source or methodology and is treated here as an unverifiable industry claim — it is not used.' In §2.1, vendor studies are explicitly labeled: 'vendor-published case studies; single deployments, marketing instruments subject to selection bias, reported without control groups or baselines'.

The paper establishes a reproducible protocol and references independent confirmations in §6: 'Independent Empirical Replication. The empirical underwriting findings independently replicate the large-scale cash-flow default reduction findings of FinRegLab (2019, 2021; N = 85,000 borrowers across 6 financial institutions) and replicate the CFPB's national error rate through automated, live REST API queries... Data availability. Simulation code, seeds, figures, and pre-registration documents are deposited at OSF / Zenodo Archive... with cryptographic SHA-256 manifest verification (SHA256_REPRODUCIBILITY_MANIFEST.json; 1,343 verified assets).'

Sampling and measurement biases are explicitly documented and controlled across both empirical citations and simulations. In §1.2, the paper contrasts non-representative volunteer samples with representative ones: 'Consumer Reports, 2024 — volunteer sample, not nationally representative; cited alongside the FTC’s representative 2013 estimate of 26%'. In §3.2, self-selection bias for the optional physiology stream is explicitly bounded: 'wearable owners differ systematically from non-owners, so the concordance pilot’s population inference carries a self-selection caveat... but this selection bias can distort the theory validation, never a user’s credit outcome.' In §3.4, simulation sampling uses randomized parameters ('300 synthetic users, true lambda ~ U[0.05, 0.95]').

Sample sizes are explicitly stated and sufficiently large to account for population variability across both synthetic batteries and empirical datasets: e.g., '300-user re-run of the estimator... Poisson cadence 0.3–3 events/day over 365 days, median 569 events per user' (§3.4), 'N = 500' for Kuramoto coherence surfaces (Figure 7), '2M files, seed 42' for Monte-Carlo PPV validation (Figure 9), 'TRIBE v2 was trained on over 1,000 hours of fMRI from 720 subjects' (§3.4), and '2,365,586 published credit-reporting complaints' (§1.2).

The methodology employs rigorous negative controls, semantic controls, and paraphrase controls in its computational experiments, while benchmarking against an explicit incumbent control group (§2.3: 'The incumbent control group: measured alternative-data results'). In §3.4: 'CLICS provides the semantic control geometry... A planted lambda = 0 negative control recovers max|lambda_hat| = 0.0092 (no phantom sensitivity)... shuffled-label negative control correctly null (p = 0.684).' In §4: 'plus two non-financial controls... and the paraphrase-controlled arm (Sim D8) gives LOO 0.40 vs 0.20 chance'.

Appropriate statistical tests are applied matching the data type alongside explicit effect sizes and practical significance thresholds. In §3.4: 'Kalman/EM state-space estimator... Mantel permutation tests score concordance between the three spaces’ distance geometries... latent trajectory recovery r = 0.879 (threshold 0.7)... planted neural x behavioral concordance detected at Mantel r = 1.0, p = 0.002; partial concordance given text p = 0.002'. Practical significance is explicitly defined via SESOI: 'The 0.15 half-width is a pre-registered smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) for an equivalence test' (§3.4), and Sim P7b reports 'monotonicity rho = 1.000 and a robust Delta U >= 0.200 protection floor' (§4, Table W11).

Randomization seeds, parameter distributions, and demographic breakdowns are fully detailed. For simulations, exact distributions and seeds are provided: '300 synthetic users, true lambda ~ U[0.05, 0.95], mixed-sign tilde{varepsilon} streams (12–15% negative, heavier-tailed betrayals), Poisson cadence 0.3–3.0 events/day over 365 days (median 569 events/user, range 112–1100)' (Figure 8), 'SIM-R1 battery 1, seed 42' (§3.4), and 'Monte-Carlo crosses (2M files, seed 42)' (Figure 9). For empirical data, demographic allocations are explicitly detailed in §1.1: 'invisibility concentrated among Black (28%) and Hispanic (26%) consumers versus 16% of White and Asian consumers, and 40% of invisibles under 25.'

Exact p-values, standard deviations, means, medians, and percentiles (p5, p95, max) are thoroughly reported throughout the text. Examples include: 'R = 0.739 ± 0.029 coupled vs. 0.040 ± 0.001 isolated' (§4), 'day 318 ± 133 at r_floor = 0.01/day' (§4.3), '|lambda_hat - lambda| mean 0.0074, p95 0.0215, max 0.0343' (§3.4), 'median r = 1.000 (p5 = 0.999, min 0.990)' (Footnote 1), 'uptake of adversarial contracts from 0.725 to 0.284 (p = 0.004)' (§3.3), and 'LOO 0.40 vs 0.20 chance, p = 0.046' (§4).

The paper explicitly commits to reporting raw counts, baselines, absolute risks, NNT, and NNH alongside relative metrics. In §1.2, exact complaint counts and bases are given: 'of the 2,365,586 published credit-reporting complaints received in 2024, incorrect information on your report accounts for 1,175,009 (49.7%) and problem with a company’s investigation into an existing problem for 455,637 (19.3%) — together 69.0%... (sum of the rounded shares; exact 68.93%)... shares do not transfer to the 2,703,400 received base, on which they are 60.3%'. In §4.3 and §4.4, dedicated NNH and NNT analyses are performed: 'The number-needed-to-harm at the flagging stage is therefore ~1.03 at 1% prevalence' (§4.3) and 'The error-correction NNT is 52 / 24 / 19 at q = 0.37 / 0.80 / 1.00' (§4.4).

While the paper notes that '25% of would-be participants could not access their own reports at all' in an external survey (§1.2) and accounts for unpublished complaints in the CFPB database, it does not present a participant flow log or explicit accounting of participant withdrawals, dropouts, or outlier exclusions for its own primary human study, as the real-user concordance pilot has not yet been executed ('What remains open, and is now the A-grade gate: the same tests on real users', §3.4).

The paper maintains strict consistency regarding what its primary outcome metric actually measures, refusing to conflate its surrogate assurance metric with true vulnerability-based trustworthiness. In the Abstract: '(§ 2.2: the score’s contract-enforced inputs are assurance-channel validations whose correlation with trustworthiness is hypothesized, not identical to it)'. In §2.2: 'A missed payment measures shock exposure and capacity at least as much as willingness... The score therefore measures calibrated compliance dynamics, which correlate with trustworthiness [HYPOTHESIS — no field correlation has been measured; the § 3.4 concordance pilot is the registered test] but are not identical to it'.

Statistical significance and model recovery metrics are explicitly separated from practical and clinical impact. In §3.4, the paper notes that passing the pre-registered SESOI equivalence corridor is statistically easy given fine instrument resolution, warning against over-interpreting statistical corroboration: 'the instrument’s demonstrated recovery error is far finer (mean 0.0074, p95 0.0215, max 0.0343; ultra-thin worst case 0.0737), so the corridor is conservative in the direction of easy corroboration — and H2 corroboration is therefore weak evidence'. Furthermore, §4.3 and §4.4 translate statistical performance (sensitivity 0.90 / specificity 0.71) into practical human impact (97 of 100 adverse flags wrong at 1% prevalence; NNH ~ 1.03).

The paper rigorously separates correlation from causation and explicitly quantifies confounding variables and observation/Hawthorne effects. In §1.5: 'the evidence is stated here with its causal strength graded rather than inflated... social isolation and loneliness are associated with elevated all-cause mortality... associations in which reverse causation is not excluded... Critically, the credit–health correlation is substantially confounded: in the Dunedin cohort (N = 1,037), human-capital factors (education, cognition, self-control) explain ~45% of the credit-score–cardiovascular-risk association... Accordingly, this document does not claim the incumbent system is a morbidity exposure.' In §1.4, observation/demand effects (Hawthorne-class effects) are explicitly analyzed: 'demand characteristics show heterogeneous, bidirectional participation effects with frequent nulls (McCambridge, 2014: 12 of 19 studies positive, 5 clear nulls)... user-owned measurement drives observation salience toward its floor but not to zero... FreshCredit’s measurement still distorts, illustratively inflating mismatch variance by ~5% at residual salience'.

Figures and captions explicitly document axis scales, baselines, and map artifacts to prevent visual distortion. In Figure 12: '(a) Fee totals (log scale)'. In Figure 7 and §4, the authors explicitly expose and avoid a mathematical mapping artifact that would visually inflate baseline coherence: 'A half-circle (arctan) phase map would inflate the K = 0 control to R approx 0.635; the incoherent baseline under the stereographic map is approx 0.03–0.05.' Figure 8, 9, 10, and 11 captions provide full parameter bounds, error bands (±0.15 certified band), and exact baseline anchors.

Hypotheses, equivalence corridors, and evaluation criteria were explicitly pre-registered before data collection/simulation runs, and failed replications or uncorrected tests are transparently disclosed rather than p-hacked. In §0, Null (H_0) and Alternative (H_1) hypotheses are stated. In §3.4: 'PRE-REGISTERED PROTOCOL (OSF / Zenodo Archive (Release v4.3...))... against pre-registered criteria frozen in code before the passing run... The P1–P3 Mantel tests are uncorrected for multiplicity'. In §4, failed arms are openly reported: 'the multilingual arms failed their frozen criteria and are reported as failed — no cross-language claim is made. A second-encoder replication attempt (Sim D9...) also failed its frozen criteria and is reported as failed'.

Simulation timeframes and follow-up horizons are logically scaled to capture long-term convergence, multi-year adoption stalls, and transitional default surges. Specifically: estimator validation runs over '365 days (median 569 events/user)' (§3.4); cold-start convergence tracks up to '563' days to asymptote (§4.3); network adoption ODEs evaluate 'adopted fraction after 10 years' (§4.1, Figure 11); and the Dynamic Lemons Market ODE (Sim W9) models 'adverse borrower selection during the initial 36-month migration from incumbent bureaus' (§5, Figure 11).

Models and trends are strictly bounded within their tested regimes, and failures outside those regimes are explicitly documented. In §2: 'normalization is window-relative and must be re-anchored when the regime shifts'. In §3.4, the authors explicitly test and refuse to extrapolate the constant-lambda estimator to an adaptive-lambda regime: 'under a Behrens-style adaptive-lambda ground truth... the constant-lambda estimator does not recover the time-average gain within the certified 0.15 tolerance... The estimator certification therefore now reads: certified for constant-lambda structure at the printed error levels... not certified for the time-average gain under adaptive truth'. In §4.4, unmeasured extrapolations are refused: 'Declared not computable without new data: the Experian-Boost-based NNT... and the global-inclusion benefit'.

Mathematical formulations and results adhere strictly to probability and dynamical stability boundaries. In the Abstract: 'regularization floor epsilon_min = 10^-4 certifying numerical stability against zero-variance history profiles'. In §3: 'trust index iota(T) = tanh(w * tilde{T}) in (-1, 1)... at neutral trust iota = 0 it reduces exactly to standard expected utility, and the distortion is bounded'. In §3.4: 'The closed-loop analysis gives lambda a natural stable range (0,1) with critical damping at lambda = 1/4... the stability boundary shrinks to (0, 0.618) under a two-step closure'. In §5, Shapley attribution achieves machine-precision conservation ('reconstruction discrepancy 1.39 x 10^-17').
